title: Sub-Gaussian Random Variable
informal: A random variable $X$ is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy $\sigma^2$ (under the measure $\mu$) if its centered moment generating function is dominated by that of a centered Gaussian of variance $\sigma^2$: $$\mathbb{E}\bigl[\exp\bigl(\lambda\,(X - \mathbb{E}X)\bigr)\bigr] \le \exp\!\left(\frac{\lambda^2 \sigma^2}{2}\right) \qquad \text{for all } \lambda \in \mathbb{R}.$$ Equivalently, the tails of $X$ decay at least as fast as those of a Gaussian. This is the foundational object from which the Markov/Chernoff bounds, Gaussian-type tail bounds, Hoeffding's inequality, and the maximal inequalities are all derived.
summary: A random variable is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy sigma-squared when its centered moment generating function is dominated by that of a centered Gaussian of variance sigma-squared.
leanSignature:
def IsSubGaussian (X : Ω → ℝ) (σ2 : ℝ≥0) (μ : Measure Ω := by volume_tac) : Prop :=
  HasSubgaussianMGF (fun ω => X ω - ∫ x, X x ∂μ) σ2 μ
formalizationNotes: Implemented as a thin bridge to Mathlib's HasSubgaussianMGF applied to the centered variable X − E[X]. For a non-integrable X the Bochner mean is Mathlib's junk value 0, in which case the definition reduces to the un-centered Mathlib predicate.

hypotheses.label: Centered MGF bound
hypotheses.note: The moment generating function of X − E[X] is bounded by exp(λ²σ²/2) for every real λ.

reference.formal: Junwei Lu, *Big Data Analysis*, Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025.
reference.biblio: The notion of a sub-Gaussian random variable is classical folklore with no single seminal origin. The terminology and the defining MGF bound trace to J.-P. Kahane, *Propriétés locales des fonctions à séries de Fourier aléatoires*, Studia Mathematica 19 (1960), and the systematic study to V. V. Buldygin and Yu. V. Kozachenko, *Sub-Gaussian random variables*, Ukrainian Mathematical Journal 32 (1980). The variance-proxy MGF formulation used here is the standard textbook synthesis (see also Wainwright, *High-Dimensional Statistics*, 2019, §2.1.2; Boucheron, Lugosi & Massart, *Concentration Inequalities*, 2013, §2.3).

title: Bounded Variables are Sub-Gaussian (Hoeffding's Lemma)
informal: If a random variable $X$ is bounded, $a \le X \le b$ almost surely, then $X$ is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy $\sigma^2 = (b-a)^2/4$. Equivalently, the centered moment generating function satisfies $$\mathbb{E}\!\left[e^{\lambda(X-\mathbb{E}X)}\right] \le \exp\!\left(\frac{\lambda^2 (b-a)^2}{8}\right), \qquad \lambda \in \mathbb{R}.$$ This is Hoeffding's lemma, the moment-generating-function control underlying Hoeffding's inequality.
summary: A random variable almost surely confined to an interval [a,b] is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy (b-a)-squared over four.
leanSignature:
theorem isSubGaussian_of_mem_Icc {X : Ω → ℝ} {a b : ℝ} {μ : Measure Ω}
    [IsProbabilityMeasure μ]
    (hm : AEMeasurable X μ)
    (hb : ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, X ω ∈ Set.Icc a b) :
    IsSubGaussian X ((‖b - a‖₊ / 2) ^ 2) μ
formalizationNotes: The book's proxy (b−a)²/4 is exactly Mathlib's (‖b−a‖₊/2)². The only added hypothesis relative to the book is a.e.-measurability of X, a regularity condition left implicit in the text.

hypotheses.label: Bounded a.s.
hypotheses.note: X lies in the interval [a, b] almost surely.

reference.formal: Junwei Lu, *Big Data Analysis*, Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025.
reference.biblio: W. Hoeffding, *Probability inequalities for sums of bounded random variables*, Journal of the American Statistical Association **58**(301), 1963, 13–30. The moment-generating-function bound for a bounded centered random variable (Hoeffding's lemma) is the key step in the proof of Theorem 2 of that paper; it is now standard textbook material and is what the variance-proxy statement formalized here records.

title: Markov's Inequality
informal: For a nonnegative integrable random variable $X$ and a threshold $t > 0$, $$\mathbb{P}(X \ge t) \;\le\; \frac{\mathbb{E}[X]}{t}.$$ The book uses the strict event $\{X > t\}$; enlarging to $\{X \ge t\}$ preserves the inequality, so the form proved here is strictly stronger.
summary: For a nonnegative integrable random variable and a positive threshold t, the probability of exceeding t is at most the mean divided by t.
leanSignature:
theorem markov
    {X : Ω → ℝ} {μ : Measure Ω} {t : ℝ}
    (hX_nn : 0 ≤ᵐ[μ] X)
    (hX_int : Integrable X μ)
    (ht : 0 < t) :
    μ.real {ω | t ≤ X ω} ≤ (∫ x, X x ∂μ) / t

hypotheses.label: Nonnegative
hypotheses.note: X is almost surely nonnegative.

hypotheses.label: Integrable
hypotheses.note: X has a finite mean.

hypotheses.label: Positive threshold
hypotheses.note: t > 0, so we may divide by t.

reference.formal: Junwei Lu, *Big Data Analysis*, Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025.
reference.biblio: *Markov's inequality* is classical folklore with no single seminal paper; it is named after A. A. Markov and generalises the bound of his teacher P. L. Chebyshev (Chebyshev, *Des valeurs moyennes*, Journal de mathématiques pures et appliquées, 1867). The Chernoff bound — optimising the exponential Markov inequality over a tilt parameter — originates with H. Chernoff (1952).

title: Chernoff Bound
informal: Let $\psi(\lambda) = \log \mathbb{E}\big[e^{\lambda(X-\mathbb{E}X)}\big]$ be the centered cumulant generating function and $\psi^*(t) = \sup_{\lambda \ge 0}\big(\lambda t - \psi(\lambda)\big)$ its Fenchel–Legendre dual. Then for every $t$, $$\mathbb{P}\big(X - \mathbb{E}X \ge t\big) \;\le\; e^{-\psi^*(t)}.$$ The bound holds provided the centered exponential moments are finite on $[0,\infty)$ and the set defining $\psi^*$ is bounded above (so the supremum is the genuine textbook one).
summary: The right deviation of a centered random variable is bounded by the exponential of minus the Fenchel-Legendre dual of its cumulant generating function.
leanSignature:
theorem chernoff
    {X : Ω → ℝ} {μ : Measure Ω} [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] {t : ℝ}
    (hInt : ∀ lam, 0 ≤ lam →
      Integrable (fun ω => Real.exp (lam * (X ω - ∫ x, X x ∂μ))) μ)
    (hBdd : BddAbove (Set.range (fun lam : {lam : ℝ // 0 ≤ lam} =>
      lam.val * t - psi X μ lam.val))) :
    μ.real {ω | t ≤ X ω - ∫ x, X x ∂μ} ≤ Real.exp (-psiStar X μ t)
formalizationNotes: The Lean statement makes no sign assumption on t (the book states it for t ≥ 0), so it is strictly stronger. The two side conditions are Lean-side guards: finiteness of the MGF on [0,∞) lets the per-λ exponential Markov step apply, and boundedness-above aligns the real-valued supremum defining ψ* with the textbook sup (otherwise it falls back on the junk value 0, making the bound vacuous).

hypotheses.label: MGF finite on [0,∞)
hypotheses.note: The centered exponential moment exp(λ(X−E X)) is integrable for every λ ≥ 0.

hypotheses.label: Dual set bounded above
hypotheses.note: The set {λt − ψ(λ) : λ ≥ 0} is bounded above, so its supremum ψ*(t) is the genuine textbook value.

reference.formal: Junwei Lu, *Big Data Analysis*, Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025.
reference.biblio: The *Chernoff bound* — optimising the exponential Markov inequality over the tilt parameter $\lambda$ — originates with H. Chernoff, *A measure of asymptotic efficiency for tests of a hypothesis based on the sum of observations*, Annals of Mathematical Statistics **23** (1952), 493–507; the exponential-rate / large-deviation argument appears there in the analysis of error probabilities (Chernoff credits the key inequality to Herman Rubin). The Legendre-dual rate function $\psi^*$ is the same object that governs Cramér's large-deviation theorem.

title: Scalar Multiple of a Sub-Gaussian Variable
informal: If $X$ is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy $\sigma^2$, then for any constant $c$ the scaled variable $c\,X$ is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy $c^2\sigma^2$. This is the elementary closure property of the sub-Gaussian class under scalar multiplication, used downstream to scale per-coordinate noise bounds in regression.
summary: Scaling a sub-Gaussian variable by a constant c gives a sub-Gaussian variable with variance proxy multiplied by c-squared.

hypotheses.label: Sub-Gaussian input
hypotheses.note: X is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy σ².

reference.formal: Junwei Lu, *Big Data Analysis*, Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025.
reference.biblio: The seminal source for the sub-Gaussian tail/MGF machinery is W. Hoeffding, *Probability inequalities for sums of bounded random variables*, Journal of the American Statistical Association **58**(301), 1963, 13–30. The scalar-multiple closure rule is elementary textbook material and appears in modern references such as Boucheron, Lugosi & Massart, *Concentration Inequalities* (2013), Vershynin, *High-Dimensional Probability* (2018), and Wainwright, *High-Dimensional Statistics* (2019).

title: Hoeffding's Inequality
informal: Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be independent random variables, each sub-Gaussian with variance proxy $\sigma^2$. Then for every threshold $t > 0$, the centered sample mean obeys $$\mathbb{P}\!\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(X_i - \mathbb{E}X_i\bigr) > t\right) \;\le\; \exp\!\left(-\frac{n\,t^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).$$ Equivalently, the centered sum $\sum_{i}(X_i - \mathbb{E}X_i)$ exceeds $nt$ with the same bound — the form stated and proved directly here (requiring at least one variable).
summary: For independent sub-Gaussian variables with common variance proxy, the centered sample mean has a Gaussian-type upper tail exp(-n t-squared / (2 sigma-squared)).
leanSignature:
theorem hoeffding {n : ℕ} {X : ℕ → Ω → ℝ} {σ2 : ℝ≥0} {μ : Measure Ω}
    [IsProbabilityMeasure μ]
    (hX_meas : ∀ i, Measurable (X i))
    (hX_indep : iIndepFun X μ)
    (hX_subG : ∀ i, i < n → IsSubGaussian (X i) σ2 μ)
    (hn : 1 ≤ n)
    {t : ℝ} (ht : 0 < t) :
    μ.real {ω | (n : ℝ) * t ≤ ∑ i ∈ Finset.range n, (X i ω - ∫ x, X i x ∂μ)}
      ≤ Real.exp (-(n : ℝ) * t ^ 2 / (2 * (σ2 : ℝ)))
formalizationNotes: Stated with the non-strict threshold nt ≤ ∑(Xᵢ−E Xᵢ) rather than the book's strict >, which is at least as strong. Measurability of each Xᵢ is a technical requirement of Mathlib's independence-transfer machinery, not a book assumption.

hypotheses.label: Independence
hypotheses.note: The variables X 0, …, X (n−1) are jointly independent.

hypotheses.label: Sub-Gaussian
hypotheses.note: Each Xᵢ is sub-Gaussian with the common variance proxy σ².

hypotheses.label: n ≥ 1
hypotheses.note: At least one variable in the family.

reference.formal: Junwei Lu, *Big Data Analysis*, Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025.
reference.biblio: The seminal source is W. Hoeffding, *Probability inequalities for sums of bounded random variables*, Journal of the American Statistical Association **58**(301), 1963, 13–30, whose Theorem 2 gives the exponential tail bound for sums of bounded independent variables. The sub-Gaussian reformulation stated here replaces the boundedness hypothesis with a sub-Gaussian variance proxy; in this generality it is textbook synthesis presented in modern references (Boucheron, Lugosi & Massart, 2013; Vershynin, *High-Dimensional Probability*, 2018; Wainwright, *High-Dimensional Statistics*, 2019).

title: Two-Sided Sub-Gaussian Tail Bound
informal: If $X$ is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy $\sigma^2$, then for every $t \ge 0$ the absolute deviation satisfies $$\mathbb{P}\bigl(\,|X - \mathbb{E}X| > t\,\bigr) \;\le\; 2\,\exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).$$ This is the standard two-sided Gaussian-type concentration of a sub-Gaussian variable around its mean, obtained by combining the one-sided Chernoff tail with a union bound over the two tails.
summary: A sub-Gaussian variable's absolute deviation from its mean exceeds t with probability at most twice exp(-t-squared / (2 sigma-squared)).
formalizationNotes: The book states the bound for t > 0; the weaker hypothesis t ≥ 0 used here yields a formally stronger statement (the t = 0 case is trivial). Finiteness of the measure is forced by the embedded HasSubgaussianMGF predicate, so no IsFiniteMeasure typeclass is required at the user surface.

hypotheses.label: Sub-Gaussian
hypotheses.note: X is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy σ².

hypotheses.label: t ≥ 0
hypotheses.note: The deviation level is nonnegative (book: t > 0).

reference.formal: Junwei Lu, *Big Data Analysis*, Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025.
reference.biblio: The two-sided sub-Gaussian tail bound is folklore: it follows immediately from the defining moment-generating-function bound by an optimized Chernoff argument and a union bound over the two tails. The modern axiomatic theory of sub-Gaussian variables — the equivalence of the MGF bound, the tail bound, and the Orlicz-norm characterization — was systematized by V. V. Buldygin and Yu. V. Kozachenko (1980); the underlying technique traces to J.-P. Kahane's study of sub-Gaussian series. Standard treatments include Wainwright, *High-Dimensional Statistics* (2019), §2.1, and Vershynin, *High-Dimensional Probability* (2018), §2.5.

title: Sub-Exponential Random Variable
informal: A random variable $X$ is sub-exponential with parameter $\alpha$ if its centered moment generating function obeys the sub-Gaussian-type bound on the restricted range $|\lambda| \le 1/\alpha$: $$\mathbb{E}\!\left[\exp\big(\lambda(X-\mathbb{E}X)\big)\right] \le \exp\!\left(\tfrac{\lambda^2 \alpha^2}{2}\right) \qquad\text{for all } |\lambda| \le \tfrac{1}{\alpha}.$$ The key difference from sub-Gaussianity is the restricted range of $\lambda$: the sub-Gaussian bound holds for all real $\lambda$, whereas the sub-exponential bound is required only on $|\lambda| \le 1/\alpha$. A second field bundles integrability of the centered exponential on that range.
summary: A random variable is sub-exponential with parameter alpha when its centered MGF obeys a Gaussian-type bound but only on the restricted range |lambda| at most 1/alpha.
leanSignature:
structure IsSubExponential (X : Ω → ℝ) (α : ℝ≥0) (μ : Measure Ω := by volume_tac) :
    Prop where
  mgf_le : ∀ l : ℝ, |l| ≤ 1 / (α : ℝ) →
    mgf (fun ω => X ω - ∫ x, X x ∂μ) μ l ≤ Real.exp (l ^ 2 * (α : ℝ) ^ 2 / 2)
  integrable_exp_mul : ∀ l : ℝ, |l| ≤ 1 / (α : ℝ) →
    Integrable (fun ω => Real.exp (l * (X ω - ∫ x, X x ∂μ))) μ
formalizationNotes: Mathlib has no predicate for the restricted-range MGF bound, so it is built here as a structure over the centered variable, mirroring HasSubgaussianMGF. The integrability field is added relative to the bare book statement so the MGF is a genuine integral rather than a junk value. The degenerate α = 0 collapses the range to λ = 0.

hypotheses.label: Restricted MGF bound
hypotheses.note: On |λ| ≤ 1/α the centered MGF is bounded by exp(λ²α²/2).

hypotheses.label: Integrability
hypotheses.note: The centered exponential is integrable on the same range, so the MGF is the genuine Bochner integral.

reference.formal: Junwei Lu, *Big Data Analysis*, Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025.
reference.biblio: The sub-exponential class via a restricted-range MGF (equivalently characterized by Orlicz $\psi_1$-norm, linear-in-$t$ MGF growth, or exponential tails) is textbook folklore with no single seminal origin; it is standard background for the Bernstein-type inequalities tracing to S. N. Bernstein (1920s). Modern treatments are R. Vershynin, *High-Dimensional Probability* (2018), §2.7–2.8, and M. J. Wainwright, *High-Dimensional Statistics* (2019), §2.1.3 (the $(\nu^2,\alpha)$-Bernstein condition).

title: Sub-Exponential Tail Bound (Quadratic Regime)
informal: If $X$ is sub-exponential with parameter $\alpha > 0$, then in the small-deviation regime $0 \le t \le \alpha$ the right tail of the centered variable decays like that of a Gaussian: $$\mathbb{P}\bigl(X - \mathbb{E}X > t\bigr) \;\le\; \exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2}{2\alpha^2}\right).$$ The crossover to the lighter linear regime occurs at $t = \alpha$, where the two bounds agree.
summary: For small deviations (t at most alpha), a sub-exponential variable's right tail decays like a Gaussian, exp(-t-squared / (2 alpha-squared)).
leanSignature:
theorem IsSubExponential.measure_sub_integral_lt_le_quadratic
    {X : Ω → ℝ} {α : ℝ≥0} {μ : Measure Ω}
    (hX : IsSubExponential X α μ)
    (hα : 0 < (α : ℝ))
    {t : ℝ} (ht : 0 ≤ t)
    (htα : t ≤ (α : ℝ)) :
    μ {ω | t < X ω - ∫ x, X x ∂μ}
      ≤ ENNReal.ofReal (Real.exp (-t ^ 2 / (2 * (α : ℝ) ^ 2)))
formalizationNotes: Proved by the Chernoff method at the optimal tilt λ = t/α² (in range since t ≤ α). The book requires t > 0; allowing t = 0 (trivial bound) gives a slightly stronger form.

hypotheses.label: Sub-exponential
hypotheses.note: X is sub-exponential with parameter α > 0.

hypotheses.label: Quadratic regime
hypotheses.note: The deviation t is at most α.

reference.formal: Junwei Lu, *Big Data Analysis*, Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025.
reference.biblio: The two-regime sub-exponential tail bound is textbook folklore: the standard packaging of the sub-exponential MGF condition into a deviation inequality via the Chernoff method. References giving this two-regime statement are R. Vershynin, *High-Dimensional Probability* (2018), §2.8, and M. J. Wainwright, *High-Dimensional Statistics* (2019), §2.1.3. The underlying Chernoff bounding technique originates with H. Chernoff (1952).

title: Sub-Exponential Tail Bound (Linear Regime)
informal: If $X$ is sub-exponential with parameter $\alpha > 0$, then in the large-deviation regime $t \ge \alpha$ the right tail exhibits the lighter, purely exponential decay $$\mathbb{P}\bigl(X - \mathbb{E}X > t\bigr) \;\le\; \exp\!\left(-\frac{t}{2\alpha}\right).$$ This is the heavy-tail regime of the sub-exponential class, where the exponential rate replaces the Gaussian one of the quadratic regime.
summary: For large deviations (t at least alpha), a sub-exponential variable's right tail decays purely exponentially, exp(-t / (2 alpha)).
leanSignature:
theorem IsSubExponential.measure_sub_integral_lt_le_linear
    {X : Ω → ℝ} {α : ℝ≥0} {μ : Measure Ω}
    (hX : IsSubExponential X α μ)
    (hα : 0 < (α : ℝ))
    {t : ℝ} (htα : (α : ℝ) ≤ t) :
    μ {ω | t < X ω - ∫ x, X x ∂μ}

hypotheses.label: Sub-exponential
hypotheses.note: X is sub-exponential with parameter α > 0.

hypotheses.label: Linear regime
hypotheses.note: The deviation t is at least α.

reference.formal: Junwei Lu, *Big Data Analysis*, Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025.
reference.biblio: The two-regime sub-exponential tail bound is textbook folklore: Gaussian decay for small deviations and exponential decay for large ones, obtained from the sub-exponential MGF condition via the Chernoff method. Standard references are R. Vershynin, *High-Dimensional Probability* (2018), §2.8, and M. J. Wainwright, *High-Dimensional Statistics* (2019), §2.1.3. The Chernoff technique originates with H. Chernoff (1952).

title: Sub-Exponential Sample-Mean Concentration (Quadratic Regime)
informal: Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be independent sub-exponential variables with common parameter $\alpha > 0$ and common mean $\mu_0$, and let $\bar X_n = \tfrac1n\sum_i X_i$. Then in the small-deviation regime $0 \le t \le \alpha$, $$\mathbb{P}\bigl(\bar X_n - \mu_0 > t\bigr) \;\le\; \exp\!\left(-\frac{n\,t^2}{2\alpha^2}\right).$$ This is the classical Bernstein-type concentration of averages of sub-exponential variables in its Gaussian-like regime.
summary: The centered sample mean of n independent sub-exponential variables has Gaussian-type decay exp(-n t-squared / (2 alpha-squared)) for small deviations.
leanSignature:
theorem measure_sampleMean_lt_le_quadratic
    {n : ℕ} (hn : 0 < n)
    {X : Fin n → Ω → ℝ} {α : ℝ≥0} {μ : Measure Ω} {μ₀ : ℝ}
    (hX : ∀ i, IsSubExponential (X i) α μ)
    (hμ₀ : ∀ i, ∫ ω, X i ω ∂μ = μ₀)
    (hindep : iIndepFun X μ)
    (hα : 0 < (α : ℝ))
    (hmeas : ∀ i, Measurable (X i))
    {t : ℝ} (ht : 0 ≤ t)
    (htα : t ≤ (α : ℝ)) :
    μ {ω | t < (1 / (n : ℝ)) * ∑ i : Fin n, X i ω - μ₀}
      ≤ ENNReal.ofReal (Real.exp (-(n : ℝ) * t ^ 2 / (2 * (α : ℝ) ^ 2)))

hypotheses.label: Sub-exponential
hypotheses.note: Each Xᵢ is sub-exponential with the common parameter α.

hypotheses.label: Common mean
hypotheses.note: Each Xᵢ has the same mean μ₀.

hypotheses.label: Independence
hypotheses.note: The Xᵢ are mutually independent.

hypotheses.label: Quadratic regime
hypotheses.note: The deviation t is at most α.

reference.formal: Junwei Lu, *Big Data Analysis*, Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025.
reference.biblio: A Bernstein-type two-regime concentration inequality with no single seminal origin. Its lineage traces to Bernstein's exponential moment inequalities (S. N. Bernstein, *Theory of Probability*, 1927) and, in the modern sub-exponential / Orlicz-norm formulation, to R. Vershynin, *High-Dimensional Probability* (2018), Thm 2.8.1 and Cor 2.8.3, and M. J. Wainwright, *High-Dimensional Statistics* (2019), Prop 2.9.

title: Sub-Exponential Sample-Mean Concentration (Linear Regime)
informal: Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be independent sub-exponential variables with common parameter $\alpha > 0$ and common mean $\mu_0$, with $\bar X_n = \tfrac1n\sum_i X_i$. Then in the large-deviation regime $t \ge \alpha$, $$\mathbb{P}\bigl(\bar X_n - \mu_0 > t\bigr) \;\le\; \exp\!\left(-\frac{n\,t}{2\alpha}\right).$$ This is the exponential-decay regime of the Bernstein-type sample-mean bound.
summary: The centered sample mean of n independent sub-exponential variables has exponential decay exp(-n t / (2 alpha)) for large deviations.
leanSignature:
theorem measure_sampleMean_lt_le_linear

    {X : Fin n → Ω → ℝ} {α : ℝ≥0} {μ : Measure Ω} {μ₀ : ℝ}
    (hX : ∀ i, IsSubExponential (X i) α μ)
    (hμ₀ : ∀ i, ∫ ω, X i ω ∂μ = μ₀)
    (hindep : iIndepFun X μ)
    (hα : 0 < (α : ℝ))
    (hmeas : ∀ i, Measurable (X i))
    {t : ℝ} (htα : (α : ℝ) ≤ t) :
    μ {ω | t < (1 / (n : ℝ)) * ∑ i : Fin n, X i ω - μ₀}
      ≤ ENNReal.ofReal (Real.exp (-(n : ℝ) * t / (2 * (α : ℝ))))
formalizationNotes: Proved by Chernoff at the clamped λ = n/α giving exp(−nt/α + n/2), then n/2 ≤ nt/(2α) (since t ≥ α) closes the bound. The book uses strict t > α; equality is permitted here.

title: Bernstein Moment Condition
informal: A real random variable $X$ that is centered, $\mathbb{E}X = 0$, with variance $\operatorname{Var}(X) = \sigma^2$, satisfies the Bernstein condition with parameter $b$ if its higher absolute moments obey $$\mathbb{E}\,|X|^k \;\le\; \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\,k!\,b^{\,k-2} \qquad\text{for all integers } k \ge 3.$$ The cases $k = 1, 2$ are omitted because they are forced by the centering and variance assumptions. Bounded variables satisfy the condition: if $|X| \le B$ then $X$ is Bernstein with parameter $B/3$.
summary: A centered variable of variance sigma-squared satisfies the Bernstein condition with parameter b when its higher absolute moments are controlled by a factorial bound.
leanSignature:
structure HasBernsteinCondition (X : Ω → ℝ) (σ2 b : ℝ≥0)
    (μ : Measure Ω := by volume_tac) : Prop where
  mean_zero : ∫ ω, X ω ∂μ = 0
  variance_eq : ∫ ω, (X ω) ^ 2 ∂μ = (σ2 : ℝ)
  moment_le : ∀ k : ℕ, 3 ≤ k →
    ∫⁻ ω, ENNReal.ofReal (|X ω| ^ k) ∂μ
      ≤ ENNReal.ofReal ((σ2 : ℝ) / 2 * (k.factorial : ℝ) * (b : ℝ) ^ (k - 2))
formalizationNotes: The moment bound uses the lower Lebesgue integral rather than the Bochner integral: for a heavy-tailed X (in L² but not Lᵏ) the Bochner integral returns junk value 0, which would make the bound hold vacuously while exp(λX) is not integrable — breaking the Bernstein-to-sub-exponential implication.

hypotheses.label: Centered
hypotheses.note: X has mean zero.

hypotheses.label: Variance σ²
hypotheses.note: The parameter σ² is the variance of X.

hypotheses.label: Moment bound
hypotheses.note: E|X|ᵏ ≤ (σ²/2) k! bᵏ⁻² for every k ≥ 3.

reference.formal: Junwei Lu, *Big Data Analysis*, Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025.
reference.biblio: The moment condition $\mathbb{E}\,|X|^k \le \tfrac12\,k!\,\sigma^2\,b^{k-2}$ is the classical *Bernstein moment condition*, named for S. N. Bernstein, who introduced this family of moment hypotheses to derive exponential tail bounds (S. N. Bernstein, *Theory of Probability*, Moscow–Leningrad, 1927, with antecedents in his 1924 work). The exact factorial form is textbook standard and appears as the Bernstein condition in Boucheron, Lugosi & Massart, *Concentration Inequalities* (2013), §2.8.

title: Bernstein Condition Implies Sub-Exponential
informal: If $X$ satisfies the Bernstein moment condition with variance $\sigma^2$ and scale $b$, then $X$ is sub-exponential with parameter $\alpha = 2(\sigma \vee b)$, where $\sigma = \sqrt{\sigma^2}$ is the standard deviation: for every $|\lambda| \le 1/\alpha$, $e^{\lambda X}$ is integrable and $$\mathbb{E}\,e^{\lambda X} \;\le\; \exp\!\bigl(\tfrac12\lambda^2\alpha^2\bigr).$$ This is the bridge from the moment condition to the moment-generating-function control used in Bernstein's inequality.
summary: A variable satisfying the Bernstein moment condition is sub-exponential with parameter 2 times the max of its standard deviation and the scale b.
leanSignature:
theorem isSubExponential_of_hasBernsteinCondition
    [IsProbabilityMeasure μ]
    (hX : Measurable X)
    (hB : HasBernsteinCondition X σ2 b μ) :
    IsSubExponential X (2 * (NNReal.sqrt σ2 ⊔ b)) μ
formalizationNotes: The provable parameter uses the standard deviation, α = 2(√σ² ⊔ b), not the naive α = 2(σ² ⊔ b) which mixes variance (quadratic units) with the linear scale b and fails when σ² > 2(σ² ⊔ b)². The proof uses the monotone-convergence route enabled by the lower-Lebesgue moment bound, avoiding power-series radius bookkeeping.

hypotheses.label: Bernstein condition
hypotheses.note: X satisfies the Bernstein moment condition with parameters σ² and b.

reference.formal: Junwei Lu, *Big Data Analysis*, Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025.
reference.biblio: Textbook folklore with no single seminal paper. The moment (Bernstein) condition and its use to bound the moment generating function trace back to S. N. Bernstein's work on probability inequalities in the 1920s–1930s (S. N. Bernstein, *The Theory of Probabilities*, Moscow–Leningrad, 1927). The modern packaging — that the Bernstein moment condition yields $\mathbb{E}\,e^{\lambda X} \le \exp(\lambda^2\alpha^2/2)$ on $|\lambda| \le 1/\alpha$ — appears, up to the variance-vs-standard-deviation convention, in Wainwright (2019), §2.1.3, and in R. Vershynin, *High-Dimensional Probability* (2018), §2.7–2.8.

title: Bernstein's Inequality
informal: Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be independent random variables, each centered with common variance $\sigma^2 > 0$ and each satisfying the Bernstein condition with parameter $b > 0$. Then the sample mean $\bar X_n = \tfrac1n\sum_i X_i$ obeys, for every $t > 0$, $$\mathbb{P}\bigl(\bar X_n > t\bigr) \;\le\; \exp\!\left(-\frac{n\,t^2}{2(\sigma^2 + b\,t)}\right).$$ The constant $\sigma^2 + b\,t$ interpolates between the sub-Gaussian regime (small $t$, constant $\sigma^2$) and the sub-exponential regime (large $t$, constant $b$).
summary: For independent variables satisfying the Bernstein condition, the sample mean exceeds t with probability at most exp(-n t-squared / (2(sigma-squared + b t))).
leanSignature:
theorem bernstein_inequality {n : ℕ} {X : Fin n → Ω → ℝ} {σ2 b : ℝ≥0} {μ : Measure Ω}
    [IsProbabilityMeasure μ]
    (hX_meas : ∀ i, Measurable (X i))
    (hX_indep : iIndepFun X μ)
    (hB : ∀ i, HasBernsteinCondition (X i) σ2 b μ)
    (hn : 0 < n)
    (hb : 0 < b)
    (hσ2 : 0 < σ2)
    {t : ℝ} (ht : 0 < t) :
    μ {ω | t < (∑ i, X i ω) / (n : ℝ)}
      ≤ ENNReal.ofReal (Real.exp (-(n : ℝ) * t ^ 2 / (2 * ((σ2 : ℝ) + (b : ℝ) * t))))
formalizationNotes: This is exactly the book's statement; the constant σ² + b t is the book's and is not relaxed. The two positivity hypotheses σ² > 0 and b > 0 are made explicit (the book carries them implicitly) to place the Chernoff tilt λ = t/(σ² + b t) strictly inside (0, 1/b). The sharp per-variable MGF bound (geometric factor 1/(1−λb) retained, not bounded by 2) is re-derived here to obtain the sharp constant.

hypotheses.note: The variables are jointly independent.

hypotheses.label: Bernstein condition
hypotheses.note: Each Xᵢ satisfies the Bernstein condition with variance σ² and scale b.

hypotheses.note: The Bernstein scale parameter is positive.

hypotheses.note: Positive deviation level.

reference.formal: Junwei Lu, *Big Data Analysis*, Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025.
reference.biblio: The inequality originates with S. N. Bernstein, *On a modification of Chebyshev's inequality and of the error formula of Laplace* (in Russian), Annals of the Scientific Institutes of Savings of Ukraine, Mathematical Section, vol. 1 (1924), 38–49; reprinted in his *Collected Works*, Vol. IV, Nauka, Moscow, 1964. Bernstein replaced the Chebyshev second-moment bound by control of all higher moments, interpolating between the sub-Gaussian and sub-exponential regimes. The two-regime tail $\exp(-nt^2/(2(\sigma^2+bt)))$ is standard textbook synthesis; see Boucheron, Lugosi & Massart, *Concentration Inequalities* (2013), §2.8, and Vershynin, *High-Dimensional Probability* (2018), Theorem 2.8.1.

title: McDiarmid's Bounded-Differences Inequality
informal: Let $X = (X_0, \dots, X_{n-1})$ be $n$ independent random variables and let $f$ satisfy the bounded-differences condition with constants $c_0, \dots, c_{n-1} \ge 0$: changing the $k$-th coordinate of the argument changes $f$ by at most $c_k$, i.e. $|f(x) - f(x_{-k}, y)| \le c_k$ for all $x$ and $y$. Then the centered evaluation has the Gaussian-style upper tail, for every $t \ge 0$, $$\mathbb{P}\bigl(f(X) - \mathbb{E}f(X) > t\bigr) \;\le\; \exp\!\left(\frac{-2t^2}{\sum_{k} c_k^2}\right).$$
summary: If a function of n independent variables changes by at most c_k when its k-th argument changes, its centered evaluation has a Gaussian-type upper tail.
leanSignature:
theorem McDiarmid
    {μ : Measure Ω} [IsProbabilityMeasure μ]
    (X : ∀ i : Fin n, Ω → β i) (hX : ∀ i : Fin n, Measurable (X i))
    (f : (Π i : Fin n, β i) → ℝ) (hf : Measurable f)
    (c : Fin n → ℝ) (hc : ∀ i, 0 ≤ c i)
    (hbd : ∀ k : Fin n, ∀ x : Π i : Fin n, β i, ∀ y : β k,
        |f x - f (Function.update x k y)| ≤ c k)
    (hX_indep : iIndepFun X μ)
    (hf_int : Integrable (f ∘ allVars X) μ)
    {t : ℝ} (ht : 0 ≤ t) :
    μ {ω | t < f (allVars X ω) - ∫ ω', f (allVars X ω') ∂μ}
      ≤ ENNReal.ofReal (Real.exp (-2 * t ^ 2 / (∑ k : Fin n, c k ^ 2)))
formalizationNotes: The book states the bound for t > 0; the weaker t ≥ 0 used here is strictly stronger. Proved via a Chernoff bound on the sub-Gaussian MGF of the Doob martingale of f(X), with proxy σ² = (∑ cₖ²)/4. The bounded-differences constants are taken nonnegative, a harmless normalization.

hypotheses.label: Bounded differences
hypotheses.note: Changing one coordinate of the argument changes f by at most cₖ.

hypotheses.label: Independence
hypotheses.note: The coordinates X₀,…,Xₙ₋₁ are mutually independent.

reference.biblio: The independent bounded-differences inequality is due to C. McDiarmid, *On the method of bounded differences*, in Surveys in Combinatorics, 1989, London Mathematical Society Lecture Note Series 141, Cambridge University Press, 1989, 148–188 (stated there as Lemma (1.2)). The underlying technique — controlling the Doob martingale of $f(X)$ via a martingale exponential bound — goes back to W. Hoeffding (1963) and K. Azuma, *Weighted sums of certain dependent random variables*, Tôhoku Mathematical Journal **19** (1967), 357–367; for this reason the result is often called the Azuma–Hoeffding bounded-differences inequality.

title: McDiarmid's Inequality (Two-Sided)
informal: Under the same hypotheses as McDiarmid's inequality — $n$ independent variables and a function with bounded differences $c_0, \dots, c_{n-1}$ — the absolute deviation obeys, for every $t \ge 0$, $$\mathbb{P}\bigl(\,|f(X) - \mathbb{E}f(X)| > t\,\bigr) \;\le\; 2\,\exp\!\left(\frac{-2t^2}{\sum_{k} c_k^2}\right).$$ This is the symmetric two-sided form obtained by a union bound over the two tails.
summary: Two-sided bounded-differences inequality: the absolute deviation of f(X) from its mean exceeds t with probability at most twice the Gaussian-type bound.
leanSignature:
theorem McDiarmid_abs
    {μ : Measure Ω} [IsProbabilityMeasure μ]
    (X : ∀ i : Fin n, Ω → β i) (hX : ∀ i : Fin n, Measurable (X i))
    (f : (Π i : Fin n, β i) → ℝ) (hf : Measurable f)
    (c : Fin n → ℝ) (hc : ∀ i, 0 ≤ c i)
    (hbd : ∀ k : Fin n, ∀ x : Π i : Fin n, β i, ∀ y : β k,
        |f x - f (Function.update x k y)| ≤ c k)
    (hX_indep : iIndepFun X μ)
    (hf_int : Integrable (f ∘ allVars X) μ)
    {t : ℝ} (ht : 0 ≤ t) :
    μ {ω | t < |f (allVars X ω) - ∫ ω', f (allVars X ω') ∂μ|}
      ≤ ENNReal.ofReal (2 * Real.exp (-2 * t ^ 2 / (∑ k : Fin n, c k ^ 2)))
formalizationNotes: The event t < |Y| splits as t < Y or t < −Y; the one-sided Chernoff bound is applied to Y = f(X) − E[f(X)] (right tail) and to −Y via the MGF-negation lemma (left tail), then combined with the union bound.

title: Finite Maximal Inequality (Tail Bound)
informal: Let $X_1, \dots, X_d$ ($d \ge 1$) be (not necessarily independent) random variables, each sub-Gaussian with variance proxy $\sigma^2$ and mean zero. Then for every $t \ge 0$, $$\mathbb{P}\!\Big(\max_{1 \le j \le d} X_j > t\Big) \;\le\; d\, e^{-t^2/(2\sigma^2)}.$$ This is the union-bound step of the finite maximal inequality.
summary: The maximum of d centered sub-Gaussian variables exceeds t with probability at most d times the single-variable Gaussian tail.
formalizationNotes: The finite max is written as the supremum over the index set (equal to the pointwise maximum for d ≥ 1). The book states t > 0; t ≥ 0 is used here. Independence is not required — only a union bound over the per-coordinate sub-Gaussian Chernoff tails.

hypotheses.label: Centered
hypotheses.note: Each Xⱼ has mean zero.

hypotheses.label: Sub-Gaussian
hypotheses.note: Each Xⱼ is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy σ².

hypotheses.label: t ≥ 0
hypotheses.note: Nonnegative deviation level (book: t > 0).

reference.formal: Junwei Lu, *Big Data Analysis*, Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025.
reference.biblio: A folklore result with no single seminal origin; the textbook prototype of the maximal-inequality-via-MGF argument. A standard reference is S. Boucheron, G. Lugosi, and P. Massart, *Concentration Inequalities* (Oxford, 2013), §2.5. The same bound appears in P. Massart, *Concentration Inequalities and Model Selection*, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 1896, Springer, 2007. The argument goes back to the classical Cramér–Chernoff method applied to the maximum.

title: Finite Maximal Inequality (Expectation Bound)
informal: Let $X_1, \dots, X_d$ ($d \ge 1$) be random variables, each sub-Gaussian with variance proxy $\sigma^2$ and mean zero, on a probability space. Then $$\mathbb{E}\!\Big[\max_{1 \le j \le d} X_j\Big] \;\le\; \sigma\sqrt{2\log d}.$$ Here $\sigma = \sqrt{\sigma^2}$. This is the classical logarithmic growth of the expected maximum of sub-Gaussian variables.
summary: The expected maximum of d centered sub-Gaussian variables is at most sigma times the square root of 2 log d.
formalizationNotes: Proved by the Jensen + MGF argument: exp(λ E[max]) ≤ E[exp(λ max)] ≤ d exp(σ²λ²/2), then optimise λ = √(2 log d / σ²). The corners σ² = 0 (each Xⱼ = 0 a.e.) and d = 1 (max = X₀, mean 0, √(2 log 1) = 0) are handled separately.

hypotheses.label: Centered
hypotheses.note: Each Xⱼ has mean zero.

hypotheses.label: Sub-Gaussian
hypotheses.note: Each Xⱼ is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy σ².

reference.biblio: A folklore result with no single seminal origin; the textbook prototype of the maximal-inequality-via-MGF argument. A standard modern reference is S. Boucheron, G. Lugosi, and P. Massart, *Concentration Inequalities* (Oxford, 2013), §2.5 (the maximal inequality $\mathbb{E}[\max_j X_j] \le \sqrt{2v\log d}$). The same bound appears in P. Massart, *Concentration Inequalities and Model Selection* (Springer, 2007).

title: ℓ²-Norm Maximal Inequality (Expectation Bound)
informal: Let $X$ be a random vector in $\mathbb{R}^d$ that is sub-Gaussian as a vector: every projection $\langle u, X\rangle$ is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy $\sigma^2\|u\|^2$. If $X$ is centered, $\mathbb{E}X = 0$, then its Euclidean norm obeys $$\mathbb{E}\,\|X\| \;\le\; 4\,\sigma\,\sqrt{d}.$$ This is the dimension-dependent control of the norm of a sub-Gaussian random vector via the discretization ($\epsilon$-net) method.
summary: The expected Euclidean norm of a sub-Gaussian random vector in R^d is at most four sigma times the square root of d.
leanSignature:
theorem l2_max_expectation
    {d : ℕ} [NeZero d]
    {μ : Measure Ω} [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] {σ2 : ℝ≥0}
    {X : Ω → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d)}
    (hcenter : ∫ ω, X ω ∂μ = 0)
    (hX : ∀ u : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d),
        IsSubGaussian (fun ω => inner ℝ u (X ω)) (σ2 * ‖u‖₊ ^ 2) μ)
    (hX_int : Integrable X μ) :
    ∫ ω, ‖X ω‖ ∂μ ≤ 4 * Real.sqrt (σ2 : ℝ) * Real.sqrt (d : ℝ)
formalizationNotes: Proved by the discretization trick: a 1/2-net of the unit ball (cardinality ≤ 5^d) reduces the norm ‖X‖ = max over the sphere to a finite maximum over the net, controlled by the finite maximal inequality; log 5 ≤ 2 gives the clean constant 4σ√d. Relative to the book, centering (E[X] = 0) and Bochner integrability of X are added; integrability is in fact implied by sub-Gaussianity in finite dimension.

hypotheses.note: The random vector X has mean zero.

hypotheses.label: Sub-Gaussian vector
hypotheses.note: Every projection ⟨u, X⟩ is sub-Gaussian with proxy σ²‖u‖².

The covering/net method goes back to classical metric-entropy arguments (Kolmogorov–Tikhomirov $\epsilon$-entropy; Sudakov–Dudley chaining). For a modern treatment see R. Vershynin, *High-Dimensional Probability* (2018), §4.4.

title: ℓ²-Norm Maximal Inequality (Tail Bound)
informal: Let $X$ be a centered sub-Gaussian random vector in $\mathbb{R}^d$ (every projection $\langle u, X\rangle$ sub-Gaussian with proxy $\sigma^2\|u\|^2$), with $\mathbb{E}X = 0$. Then for every $\delta > 0$, with probability at least $1-\delta$, $$\|X\| \;\le\; 4\,\sigma\,\sqrt{d} + 2\,\sigma\,\sqrt{2\log(1/\delta)}.$$ Equivalently, the event $\{\,4\sigma\sqrt{d} + 2\sigma\sqrt{2\log(1/\delta)} < \|X\|\,\}$ has probability at most $\delta$.
summary: With probability at least 1 minus delta, the Euclidean norm of a sub-Gaussian random vector is at most four sigma root-d plus two sigma root of 2 log(1/delta).

    {X : Ω → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d)}

title: ε-Net
informal: In a (pseudo-)metric space $(X, d)$, a subset $N \subseteq s$ is an $\varepsilon$-net of $s$ if $N \subseteq s$ (the net lies inside $s$) and every point of $s$ is within distance $\varepsilon$ of some point of $N$: $$\forall\, x \in s,\ \exists\, y \in N,\ d(x, y) \le \varepsilon.$$ Also called an internal $\varepsilon$-cover. For $\varepsilon < 0$ the condition is unsatisfiable (forcing $s = \emptyset$); for $\varepsilon = 0$ in a metric space it forces $N = s$.
summary: A subset N of s is an epsilon-net when N lies inside s and every point of s is within distance epsilon of some point of N.
leanSignature:
def IsEpsilonNet (N : Set X) (s : Set X) (ε : ℝ) : Prop :=
  N ⊆ s ∧ ∀ x ∈ s, ∃ y ∈ N, dist x y ≤ ε

hypotheses.label: Internal
hypotheses.note: The net lies inside s.

hypotheses.leanToken: ∀ x ∈ s, ∃ y ∈ N, dist x y ≤ ε
hypotheses.label: Covering
hypotheses.note: Every point of s is within distance ε of some net point.

reference.formal: Junwei Lu, *Big Data Analysis*, Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025.
reference.biblio: The notions of $\varepsilon$-net, covering number, and the dual packing/capacity numbers originate with A. N. Kolmogorov and V. M. Tikhomirov, *ε-entropy and ε-capacity of sets in function spaces*, Uspekhi Matematicheskikh Nauk **14** (1959), no. 2, 3–86, where $\log_2 N(s, d, \varepsilon)$ is introduced as the $\varepsilon$-entropy (metric entropy) of $s$. The vocabulary is now standard in empirical-process and high-dimensional statistics — see also M. J. Wainwright, *High-Dimensional Statistics* (2019), §5.1.

title: Covering Number
informal: The covering number $N(s, d, \varepsilon)$ of a set $s$ in a metric space is the smallest cardinality of a finite $\varepsilon$-net of $s$: $$N(s, d, \varepsilon) \;=\; \min\bigl\{\, |N| : N \subseteq s \text{ is a finite } \varepsilon\text{-net of } s \,\bigr\},$$ taken to be $+\infty$ when no finite $\varepsilon$-net exists. It is non-increasing in $\varepsilon$: a smaller radius requires (weakly) more centres.
summary: The covering number N(s,d,epsilon) is the smallest cardinality of a finite internal epsilon-net of s.
leanSignature:
noncomputable def coveringNumber (s : Set X) (ε : ℝ) : ℕ∞ :=

formalizationNotes: A thin alias of Mathlib's Metric.coveringNumber with the radius coerced via Real.toNNReal, which clamps ε ≤ 0 to 0; for ε = 0 this equals the set's cardinality (every point is its own centre).

title: Covering Number of the ℓ²-Unit Ball
informal: For a dimension $d \ge 1$ and a radius $\varepsilon \in (0, 1)$, the covering number of the closed Euclidean unit ball $B = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^d : \|x\|_2 \le 1\}$ is bounded by $$N(B, \|\cdot\|_2, \varepsilon) \;\le\; \left(1 + \frac{2}{\varepsilon}\right)^{d}.$$ This is the standard volume/packing estimate for the $\ell^2$ ball; in the formalization the right-hand side carries a floor, since the covering number is an extended-natural-number quantity.
summary: The covering number of the Euclidean unit ball in R^d at radius epsilon is at most (1 + 2/epsilon)^d.

title: Expected Prediction MSE of Ordinary Least Squares
informal:
Consider the fixed-design linear model $Y = X\beta^\star + \varepsilon$ with design matrix $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$. Suppose the noise coordinates $\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_n$ are jointly independent, each has mean zero, and each is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy $\sigma^2$. Let $\hat\beta$ be any ordinary least-squares minimizer of $\lVert Y - X\beta\rVert^2$. Then the expected in-sample prediction error satisfies

$$\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathrm{MSE}(X\hat\beta, X\beta^\star)\right] = \frac{1}{n}\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\lVert X\hat\beta - X\beta^\star\rVert^2\right] \;\le\; \frac{\sigma^2\,\mathrm{rank}(X)}{n}.$$
summary: For the linear model with independent mean-zero sub-Gaussian noise of proxy sigma squared, the expected in-sample prediction MSE of any OLS estimator is at most sigma squared times the rank of X over n.

The only added hypothesis beyond the genuine model inputs is $n > 0$, needed so the $1/n$ factor and the right-hand side are well-defined.

title: High-Probability MSE of Ordinary Least Squares
informal:
Consider the linear model $Y = X\beta^\star + \varepsilon$ on $n$ observations, where the noise coordinates are jointly independent, centered, and each sub-Gaussian with variance proxy $\sigma^2$, and $X$ has rank $r$. Let $\hat\beta$ be any ordinary least-squares minimizer. Then for any confidence level $\delta \in (0,1)$, with probability at least $1-\delta$,

$$\mathrm{MSE}(X\hat\beta) \;\le\; \frac{32\,\sigma^2 r}{n} \;+\; \frac{16\,\sigma^2}{n}\,\log\!\Big(\tfrac1\delta\Big).$$
summary: Under independent mean-zero sub-Gaussian noise, with probability at least 1 minus delta the OLS prediction MSE is bounded by an explicit multiple of sigma squared times rank over n plus a log(1/delta) term.

title: Deterministic ℓ²-Rate of the Lasso
informal:
Consider the fixed-design linear model $Y = X\beta^\star + \varepsilon$ with $\beta^\star$ supported on a set $S$ of size $s = |S|$. Let $\hat\beta$ minimize the Lasso objective $\tfrac{1}{2n}\lVert Y - X\beta\rVert_2^2 + \lambda\lVert\beta\rVert_1$. Suppose the design satisfies the restricted eigenvalue condition $\mathrm{RE}(\kappa,3)$, i.e. $\tfrac1n\lVert X\Delta\rVert_2^2 \ge \kappa\lVert\Delta\rVert_2^2$ for every $\Delta$ in the cone $\{\lVert\Delta_{S^c}\rVert_1 \le 3\lVert\Delta_S\rVert_1\}$, and choose $\lambda \ge \tfrac{2}{n}\lVert X^\top\varepsilon\rVert_\infty$. Then the estimation error obeys the deterministic bound

$$\lVert\hat\beta - \beta^\star\rVert_2 \;\le\; \frac{3}{\kappa}\,\sqrt{s}\,\lambda.$$

No distributional assumption is placed on the noise.
summary: Under the restricted eigenvalue condition and a tuning parameter dominating twice the empirical noise score, the Lasso estimation error in ℓ² is at most three over kappa times square root of s times lambda.

title: Lasso Support Recovery: ℓ∞ Error Bound
informal:
Under the lower-eigenvalue condition (A3), mutual-incoherence condition (A4), $\alpha \in [0,1)$, and the regularization condition on $\lambda$, every Lasso minimizer $\hat\beta$ satisfies the $\ell_\infty$ error bound on the support coordinates

$$\bigl\lVert\hat\beta_S - \theta^\star_S\bigr\rVert_\infty \;\le\; B(\lambda; X),$$

where $B(\lambda; X)$ is the support-recovery bound built from the regularization level and design.
summary: Under the same conditions, every Lasso minimizer satisfies the ℓ-infinity error bound on the support coordinates, controlled by the support-recovery bound B(lambda; X).

    linfNorm (restrict S (βhat - θstar)) ≤ supportRecoveryBound X S w lam

title: Lasso Support Recovery: No False Exclusion
informal: Under the lower-eigenvalue condition (A3), mutual-incoherence condition (A4), $\alpha \in [0,1)$, and the regularization condition on $\lambda$, the Lasso recovers every sufficiently large signal coordinate: if $i \in S$ and $|\theta^\star_i| > B(\lambda; X)$, then $\hat\beta_i \neq 0$. In particular, when $\min_{i\in S}|\theta^\star_i| > B(\lambda; X)$ the Lasso achieves exact variable-selection consistency, $\operatorname{supp}(\hat\beta) = S$.
summary: Under the same conditions, every true support coordinate whose magnitude exceeds the recovery bound is selected by the Lasso, giving exact variable-selection consistency when the minimum signal exceeds the bound.

title: Lasso Support Recovery under sub-Gaussian Noise
informal:
Consider the sparse model $y = X\theta^\star + w$ with $S$-sparse signal $\theta^\star$, $|S| = s$, $s < d$. Assume the lower-eigenvalue condition (A3) with $c_{\min} > 0$, the mutual-incoherence condition (A4) with $\alpha < 1$, the $C$-column-normalization $\lVert X_j\rVert_2 \le C\sqrt n$, and that the noise components $w_1,\dots,w_n$ are independent, zero-mean, and $\sigma$-sub-Gaussian. With the regularization choice $\lambda_n = \tfrac{2C\sigma}{1-\alpha}\bigl(\sqrt{2\log(d-s)/n} + \delta\bigr)$, with probability at least $1 - 4e^{-n\delta^2/2}$ the Lasso solution has support contained in $S$ (no false inclusion) and satisfies the $\ell_\infty$ bound

$$\bigl\lVert(\hat\beta - \theta^\star)_S\bigr\rVert_\infty \le \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{c_{\min}}}\bigl(\sqrt{2\log s/n} + \delta\bigr) + \bigl\lVert(X_S^\top X_S/n)^{-1}\bigr\rVert_\infty\,\lambda_n.$$

title: The Cone Theorem for Basis Pursuit
informal:
Let $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ be a design matrix and $S \subseteq \{1,\dots,d\}$ a support set. Basis pursuit recovers a target $\beta^\star$ as the $\ell_1$-minimizer among all coefficients consistent with the observations $X\beta^\star$. Then basis pursuit has $\beta^\star$ as its unique solution for every $\beta^\star$ supported on $S$ if and only if

$$\mathcal{C}(S) \cap \mathrm{Null}(X) = \{0\},$$

where $\mathcal{C}(S) = \{\Delta : \lVert\Delta_{S^c}\rVert_1 \le \lVert\Delta_S\rVert_1\}$ is the descent cone and $\mathrm{Null}(X)$ is the kernel of $X$.
summary: Basis pursuit uniquely recovers every S-supported target if and only if the descent cone C(S) meets the null space of X only at the origin.
leanSignature:
theorem basisPursuit_unique_iff_cone_inter_ker
    (X : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin d) ℝ) (S : Finset (Fin d)) :
    (∀ βstar : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d), (∀ i ∉ S, βstar.ofLp i = 0) →
        IsUniqueBasisPursuit X (designMap X βstar) βstar)
    ↔ reCone S 1 ∩ (LinearMap.ker (designMap X) : Set (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d))) = {0}
formalizationNotes: The descent cone $\mathcal{C}(S)$ is `reCone S 1`, the factor-1 form of the general cone; $\mathrm{Null}(X)$ is the kernel of the design map. No constants are changed relative to the book.

hypotheses.note: Basis pursuit recovers each S-supported target as its unique solution.

hypotheses.label: descent cone
hypotheses.note: The cone of vectors whose off-support ell-1 mass is at most the on-support mass.

hypotheses.note: The kernel of the design map X.

reference.formal: Junwei Lu, *Big Data Analysis*, Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025.

Its equivalence with exact $\ell_1$ recovery of all $S$-supported vectors was established by A. Cohen, W. Dahmen, and R. DeVore, "Compressed sensing and best $k$-term approximation," *Journal of the American Mathematical Society*, vol. 22, no. 1, pp. 211–231, 2009. An earlier exact-recovery criterion via an uncertainty principle appears in D. L. Donoho and X. Huo, "Uncertainty principles and ideal atomic decomposition," *IEEE Transactions on Information Theory*, vol. 47, no. 7, pp. 2845–2862, 2001.

title: Perfect Recovery under the Restricted Isometry Property
informal: Let $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ be a measurement matrix and let $\beta^\star$ be an $s$-sparse signal observed through $Y = X\beta^\star$. Suppose $X$ satisfies the $3s$-Restricted Isometry Property with constant $\delta_{3s}$, i.e. for every $3s$-sparse vector $v$, $(1-\delta_{3s})\lVert v\rVert_2^2 \le \lVert Xv\rVert_2^2 \le (1+\delta_{3s})\lVert v\rVert_2^2$, and $\delta_{3s} < 1/3$. Then the basis-pursuit program ($\ell_1$-minimization subject to $X\beta = Y$) recovers $\beta^\star$ exactly: $\beta^\star$ is the unique minimizer.
summary: If the design satisfies the 3s-restricted isometry property with constant below 1/3, then basis pursuit exactly and uniquely recovers every s-sparse signal.

title: Random Gaussian Matrices Satisfy RIP with High Probability
informal:
Let $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ be a random matrix whose entries are independent and identically distributed as $N(0, 1/n)$. If the sample size satisfies $n \ge \tfrac{384}{\delta^2}\,s\,\log(18d/\varepsilon)$, then with probability at least $1 - \varepsilon$ the matrix $X$ satisfies the restricted isometry property of order $3s$ with constant $\delta$: for every $3s$-sparse vector $\beta$,

$$(1-\delta)\lVert\beta\rVert^2 \le \lVert X\beta\rVert^2 \le (1+\delta)\lVert\beta\rVert^2.$$
summary: An iid N(0,1/n) Gaussian matrix with sample size of order s log(d/epsilon) over delta squared satisfies the order-3s restricted isometry property with constant delta with probability at least 1 minus epsilon.

title: M-Estimator Regularizer Bound
informal:
Consider the regularized M-estimator $\hat\theta \in \arg\min_\theta\{\mathcal{L}(\theta) + \lambda\Phi(\theta)\}$, where $\mathcal{L}$ is convex and differentiable, $\Phi$ is a decomposable regularizer relative to a subspace pair $(M, \overline M)$, and $\lambda > 0$. Suppose $\hat\theta$ minimizes $\mathcal{L} + \lambda\Phi$ and the good event $\Phi^*(\nabla\mathcal{L}(\theta^\star)) \le \lambda/2$ holds. Then

$$\Phi(\hat\theta - \theta^\star) \;\le\; 4\bigl(\Psi(\overline M)\,\lVert\hat\theta - \theta^\star\rVert + \Phi(\theta^\star_{M^\perp})\bigr),$$

where $\Psi(\overline M)$ is the subspace-Lipschitz constant and $\Phi(\theta^\star_{M^\perp})$ is the approximation error. This requires only the good event and decomposability — no restricted strong convexity.
summary: For a convex differentiable loss with decomposable regularizer, on the good event the regularizer of the estimation error is bounded by four times the subspace-Lipschitz term plus the approximation error.

    (hG : GoodEvent dr.Φstar (gradient L θstar) lam) :
    dr.Φ (θhat - θstar) ≤
      4 * (subspaceLip dr.Φ dr.Mbar * ‖θhat - θstar‖ + dr.Φ ((dr.M)ᗮ.starProjection θstar))

title: M-Estimator Squared-Error Bound
informal:
Consider the regularized M-estimator with convex, differentiable loss $\mathcal{L}$ and decomposable regularizer $\Phi$. Suppose $\hat\theta$ minimizes $\mathcal{L} + \lambda\Phi$, the good event $\Phi^*(\nabla\mathcal{L}(\theta^\star)) \le \lambda/2$ holds, and $\mathcal{L}$ satisfies restricted strong convexity with curvature $\kappa$, radius $R$, and tolerance $\tau^2 \ge 0$. Provided $\tau^2\,\Psi^2(\overline M) \le \kappa/128$ and $\varepsilon_n^2 \le R^2$,

$$\lVert\hat\theta - \theta^\star\rVert^2 \le \varepsilon_n^2 := 144\,\frac{\lambda^2}{\kappa^2}\Psi^2(\overline M) + \frac{32}{\kappa}\Bigl(\lambda\,\Phi(\theta^\star_{M^\perp}) + 16\,\tau^2\,\Phi(\theta^\star_{M^\perp})^2\Bigr).$$

informal:
Consider a sparse generalized linear model whose response follows an exponential family with natural parameter $\langle x_i, \theta^\star\rangle$, where $\theta^\star$ is supported on a set $S$ of size $s$. The GLM negative log-likelihood is $L_n(\theta) = \tfrac1n\sum_i[\psi(\langle x_i,\theta\rangle) - y_i\langle x_i,\theta\rangle]$, and $\hat\theta$ minimizes $L_n(\theta) + \lambda\lVert\theta\rVert_1$. Assume the columns are normalized at level $C$, the loss satisfies restricted strong convexity at $\theta^\star$ with curvature $\kappa$, and $\lambda = 4BC(\sqrt{\log d/n} + \delta)$. Then with probability at least $1 - 2e^{-2n\delta^2}$,

$$\lVert\hat\theta - \theta^\star\rVert_2^2 \le 144\,\frac{\lambda^2}{\kappa^2}\,s \quad\text{and}\quad \lVert\hat\theta - \theta^\star\rVert_1 \le 48\,\frac{\lambda}{\kappa}\,s.$$

    (hlam : lam = 4 * M.B * C * (Real.sqrt (Real.log d / n) + δ))

        ≤ glmCost M ω θ + lam * l1Norm θ) :
    ENNReal.ofReal (1 - 2 * Real.exp (-2 * (n : ℝ) * δ ^ 2)) ≤
      μ {ω | ‖θhat ω - M.θstar‖ ^ 2 ≤ 144 * (lam ^ 2 / κ ^ 2) * (S.card : ℝ)
          ∧ l1Norm (θhat ω - M.θstar) ≤ 48 * (lam / κ) * (S.card : ℝ)}

The RSC condition (9.62) enters as a USER-INPUT hypothesis — the book establishes it separately (Theorem 9.36 for sub-Gaussian covariates), out of scope for this file.

With the same tuning $\lambda = 4BC(\sqrt{\log d/n} + \delta)$ and $\hat\theta$ minimizing the GLM Lasso objective, the estimator satisfies, with probability at least $1 - 2e^{-2n\delta^2}$,

$$\lVert\hat\theta - \theta^\star\rVert_\infty \;\le\; \frac{3\lambda}{\kappa}.$$

title: Benjamini–Hochberg FDR Control (Independence)
informal:
Test $N$ null hypotheses from p-values $p_1,\dots,p_N$. The Benjamini–Hochberg procedure at level $\alpha$ rejects the set $\{\, j : p_j \le \hat k\,\alpha/N \,\}$, where $\hat k = \max\{\, k \le N : \#\{\, j : p_j \le k\alpha/N \,\} \ge k \,\}$.

If the p-values are jointly independent and every null p-value is super-uniform, i.e. $\mathbb{P}(p_j \le t) \le t$ for all $t \ge 0$ and $j$ in the null set $H_0$, then the procedure controls the false discovery rate $\mathrm{FDR} = \mathbb{E}[V/(R \vee 1)]$:

$$\mathrm{FDR} \;\le\; \frac{N_0}{N}\,\alpha \;\le\; \alpha,$$ where $N_0 = |H_0|$ is the number of true nulls.
summary: Under joint independence and super-uniform null p-values, the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure at level alpha controls the false discovery rate by N0/N times alpha.
leanSignature:
theorem benjamini_hochberg_fdr_le {N : ℕ} (hN : 0 < N) (α : ℝ) (hα : 0 < α)
    (μ : Measure Ω) [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] (H₀ : Finset (Fin N)) (p : Fin N → Ω → ℝ)
    (hmeas : ∀ j, Measurable (p j))
    (hindep : iIndepFun p μ)
    (hnull : ∀ j ∈ H₀, SuperUniform (p j) μ) :
    FDR H₀ (bhRejects α p) μ ≤ (H₀.card : ℝ) / N * α
formalizationNotes: The book (Lu §20.2, Candès L7 §7.2 Thm 2) states the equality FDR = (N0/N)·α for exactly-uniform null p-values; the Lean statement proves the honest inequality ≤, which holds under the weaker super-uniform hypothesis and specializes to the book's equality when the nulls are exactly uniform. Measurability of each p-value is added as a routine Lean-only hypothesis for integration.

hypotheses.label: independence
hypotheses.note: The p-values p_1,…,p_N are jointly independent under μ.

hypotheses.label: super-uniform nulls
hypotheses.note: Every null p-value is super-uniform: P(p_j ≤ t) ≤ t for all t ≥ 0 and j ∈ H₀.

reference.formal: Junwei Lu, *Big Data Analysis*, Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025.
reference.biblio: The procedure and the FDR-control guarantee originate with Y. Benjamini and Y. Hochberg, "Controlling the false discovery rate: a practical and powerful approach to multiple testing", *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B* **57**(1) (1995), 289–300. That paper introduces the false discovery rate as an error criterion and proves (its Theorem 1) that for independent test statistics the procedure controls the FDR at level $(m_0/m)\,q \le q$, where $m_0$ is the number of true null hypotheses among $m$ tests and $q$ is the chosen level — exactly the bound formalized here.

title: Benjamini–Yekutieli FDR Control (Arbitrary Dependence)
informal:
Run the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure at level $\alpha$ on p-values $p_1,\dots,p_N$ with null index set $H_0$ of size $N_0 = |H_0|$.

If every null p-value is super-uniform, $\mathbb{P}(p_i \le t) \le t$ for all $t \ge 0$ and $i \in H_0$, and the p-values are otherwise arbitrarily dependent (no independence or positive-dependence condition), then

$$\mathrm{FDR} \;\le\; \frac{N_0}{N}\,\alpha\,H_N, \qquad H_N = \sum_{k=1}^{N} \frac1k,$$ where $H_N$ is the $N$-th harmonic number. Consequently, running BH at the deflated level $\alpha/H_N$ controls FDR at $(N_0/N)\,\alpha \le \alpha$ — the Benjamini–Yekutieli correction.
summary: Without any independence assumption, the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure controls FDR by N0/N times alpha times the N-th harmonic number; running at the deflated level alpha/H_N restores control at alpha.
leanSignature:
theorem benjamini_hochberg_dependent_fdr_le {N : ℕ} (hN : 0 < N) (α : ℝ) (hα : 0 < α)
    (μ : Measure Ω) [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] (H₀ : Finset (Fin N)) (p : Fin N → Ω → ℝ)
    (hmeas : ∀ j, Measurable (p j))
    (hnull : ∀ j ∈ H₀, SuperUniform (p j) μ) :
    FDR H₀ (bhRejects α p) μ ≤ (H₀.card : ℝ) / N * α * (harmonic N : ℝ)
formalizationNotes: The constant N0/N · α · H_N is the book constant with no deviation. The Lean statement adds only that each p-value is measurable; crucially it carries no independence hypothesis, this being the arbitrary-dependence theorem.

hypotheses.label: super-uniform nulls
hypotheses.note: Every null p-value is super-uniform: P(p_i ≤ t) ≤ t for all t ≥ 0 and i ∈ H₀.

reference.formal: E. J. Candès, *STAT 300C: Theory of Statistics*, Lecture Notes, Stanford University.
reference.biblio: The arbitrary-dependence bound is due to Y. Benjamini and D. Yekutieli, "The control of the false discovery rate in multiple testing under dependency," *Annals of Statistics* **29**(4) (2001), 1165–1188. Their Theorem 1.3 establishes $\mathrm{FDR} \le (m_0/m)\,q\,\sum_{i=1}^{m} 1/i$ for the linear step-up (BH) procedure under any joint distribution of the test statistics, and Theorem 1.4 gives the corresponding deflated-level correction. The underlying BH procedure originates with Y. Benjamini and Y. Hochberg, "Controlling the false discovery rate: a practical and powerful approach to multiple testing," *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B* **57**(1) (1995), 289–300.

title: Benjamini–Hochberg FDR Exact Identity
informal:
Consider the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure at level $\alpha$ with $0 < \alpha \le 1$ and $N$ hypotheses, of which the subset $H_0$ (with $N_0 = |H_0|$) are true nulls.

If the p-values are jointly independent and every null p-value is exactly uniform on $[0,1]$, i.e. $\mathbb{P}(p_i \le t) = t$ for $t \in [0,1]$ (not merely super-uniform), then the procedure attains FDR control with equality:

$$ \mathrm{FDR} = \frac{N_0}{N}\,\alpha. $$

This is the exact-identity companion to the super-uniform inequality $\mathrm{FDR} \le (N_0/N)\alpha$.
summary: With independent and exactly uniform null p-values, the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure attains FDR control with equality, FDR = N0/N times alpha.
leanSignature:
theorem benjamini_hochberg_fdr_eq {N : ℕ} (hN : 0 < N) {α : ℝ} (hα0 : 0 < α) (hα1 : α ≤ 1)
    (μ : Measure Ω) [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] (H₀ : Finset (Fin N)) (p : Fin N → Ω → ℝ)
    (hmeas : ∀ j, Measurable (p j))
    (hindep : iIndepFun p μ)
    (hnull : ∀ j ∈ H₀, ∀ t : ℝ, 0 ≤ t → t ≤ 1 → μ {ω | p j ω ≤ t} = ENNReal.ofReal t) :
    FDR H₀ (bhRejects α p) μ = (H₀.card : ℝ) / N * α
formalizationNotes: The lecture proves this via a backwards-martingale and Doob's optional stopping on V(t)/t; the Lean proof obtains the same identity by the leave-one-out argument, avoiding continuous-time martingale machinery absent from Mathlib. The constraint α ≤ 1 ensures every threshold kα/N lies in [0,1] so exact uniformity applies.

hypotheses.label: independence
hypotheses.note: The p-values are jointly independent under μ.

hypotheses.label: exactly uniform nulls
hypotheses.note: Every null p-value is exactly uniform on [0,1]: P(p_j ≤ t) = t for t ∈ [0,1].

reference.formal: E. J. Candès, *STAT 300C: Theory of Statistics*, Lecture Notes, Stanford University.
reference.biblio: The BH procedure and the exact independent-null identity originate with Y. Benjamini and Y. Hochberg, "Controlling the false discovery rate: a practical and powerful approach to multiple testing", *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B* **57**(1):289–300, 1995; their Theorem 1 states $\mathrm{FDR} = (m_0/m)\,q$ for independent test statistics with uniformly distributed nulls. The martingale / optional-stopping reformulation underlying the lecture proof is due to J. D. Storey, J. E. Taylor and D. Siegmund, "Strong control, conservative point estimation and simultaneous conservative consistency of false discovery rates: a unified approach", *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B* **66**(1):187–205, 2004.

title: Holm Step-Down FWER Control
informal:
Test $N$ hypotheses with one p-value $p_j$ each; let $H_0$ be the true null set with $N_0 = |H_0|$. The Holm step-down procedure sorts $p_{(1)} \le \cdots \le p_{(N)}$, compares $p_{(i)}$ against the descending cutoffs $\alpha/(N-i+1)$, and rejects the longest initial run that stays at or below its cutoff.

If every null marginal is super-uniform, $\mathbb{P}(p_j \le t) \le t$ for all $t \ge 0$ whenever $j \in H_0$, then the procedure controls the family-wise error rate $\mathrm{FWER} = \mathbb{P}(R \cap H_0 \ne \varnothing)$:

$$ \mathrm{FWER} \le \alpha. $$

No independence assumption is required.
summary: Under super-uniform null marginals, the Holm step-down procedure at level alpha controls the family-wise error rate at alpha, with no independence assumption.
leanSignature:
theorem holm_fwer_le {N : ℕ} (hN : 0 < N) (α : ℝ) (hα : 0 < α) (μ : Measure Ω)
    [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] (H₀ : Finset (Fin N)) (hH₀ : H₀.Nonempty) (p : Fin N → Ω → ℝ)
    (hmeas : ∀ j, Measurable (p j))
    (hnull : ∀ j ∈ H₀, SuperUniform (p j) μ) :
    FWER H₀ (holmRejects α p) μ ≤ ENNReal.ofReal α
formalizationNotes: Lu, Big Data Analysis states the plain Bonferroni correction but contains no Holm step-down theorem; the Holm result is formalized from Holm (1979). The Lean definitions use 0-indexed sorted positions, so the cutoff is written α/(N−i) rather than the 1-indexed α/(N−i+1); the two describe the same procedure.

hypotheses.label: super-uniform nulls
hypotheses.note: Every null marginal is super-uniform: P(p_j ≤ t) ≤ t for all t ≥ 0 and j ∈ H₀.

reference.formal: Junwei Lu, *Big Data Analysis*, Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025.
reference.biblio: The step-down procedure and its FWER guarantee are due to S. Holm, "A simple sequentially rejective multiple test procedure", *Scandinavian Journal of Statistics* **6** (1979), no. 2, 65–70; the level-$\alpha$ FWER control formalized here is Holm's Theorem 1. The companion Bonferroni correction rests on Boole's inequality, commonly attributed to C. E. Bonferroni, "Teoria statistica delle classi e calcolo delle probabilità", *Pubblicazioni del R. Istituto Superiore di Scienze Economiche e Commerciali di Firenze* **8** (1936), 3–62; its use as a multiple-comparison correction was popularized by O. J. Dunn, "Multiple comparisons among means", *Journal of the American Statistical Association* **56** (1961), no. 293, 52–64.

title: Bonferroni FWER Control
informal:
The Bonferroni correction rejects every hypothesis with $p_j \le \alpha/N$. Let $H_0$ be the true null set with $N_0 = |H_0|$.

If every null marginal is super-uniform, $\mathbb{P}(p_j \le t) \le t$ for all $t \ge 0$ whenever $j \in H_0$, then this controls the family-wise error rate:

$$ \mathrm{FWER} \le \tfrac{N_0}{N}\,\alpha \le \alpha. $$
summary: Rejecting every hypothesis with p-value at most alpha/N controls the family-wise error rate by N0/N times alpha, hence by alpha.
leanSignature:
theorem bonferroni_fwer_le {N : ℕ} (hN : 0 < N) (α : ℝ) (hα : 0 < α) (μ : Measure Ω)
    [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] (H₀ : Finset (Fin N)) (p : Fin N → Ω → ℝ)
    (hmeas : ∀ j, Measurable (p j))
    (hnull : ∀ j ∈ H₀, SuperUniform (p j) μ) :
    FWER H₀ (bonferroniRejects α p) μ ≤ ENNReal.ofReal ((H₀.card : ℝ) / N * α)
formalizationNotes: The Lean statement records the sharper N0/N·α bound; the textbook α bound follows since N0 ≤ N.

hypotheses.label: super-uniform nulls
hypotheses.note: Every null marginal is super-uniform: P(p_j ≤ t) ≤ t for all t ≥ 0 and j ∈ H₀.

reference.formal: Junwei Lu, *Big Data Analysis*, Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025.
reference.biblio: The Bonferroni correction rests on Boole's inequality (the union bound), commonly attributed to C. E. Bonferroni, "Teoria statistica delle classi e calcolo delle probabilità", *Pubblicazioni del R. Istituto Superiore di Scienze Economiche e Commerciali di Firenze* **8** (1936), 3–62; its use as a multiple-comparison correction was popularized by O. J. Dunn, "Multiple comparisons among means", *Journal of the American Statistical Association* **56** (1961), no. 293, 52–64. The single-step Bonferroni bound itself is essentially folklore.

title: Knock-off Filter FDR Control
informal:
The knock-off filter at level $\alpha$ selects variables from knock-off statistics $W = (W_1,\dots,W_d)$ (large positive $W_j$ flags a true signal, $W_j$ near zero or negative flags a null). It chooses the data-dependent threshold $t^\star$ — the smallest $t$ keeping the estimated false discovery proportion at or below $\alpha$, estimating false rejections by the number of negative statistics clearing the threshold — and rejects the variables with $W_j \ge t^\star$.

If $W$ satisfies the knock-off-score sign-symmetry assumption, with the regularity conditions that each null statistic is almost surely nonzero and the magnitudes $|W_i|$ are almost surely pairwise distinct, then the procedure controls the false discovery rate:

$$ \mathrm{FDR} = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathrm{FDP}(t^\star)\right] \le \alpha . $$
summary: Under the sign-symmetry assumption on the knock-off statistics, the knock-off+ procedure at level alpha controls the false discovery rate at alpha.
leanSignature:
theorem knockoff_fdr_le (μ : Measure Ω) [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] (α : ℝ) (hα : 0 < α)
    (W : Fin d → Ω → ℝ) (H₀ : Finset (Fin d)) (hW : KnockoffScore W H₀ μ)
    (hties : ∀ j ∈ H₀, ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, W j ω ≠ 0)
    (hmag : ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, ∀ i j : Fin d, i ≠ j → |W i ω| ≠ |W j ω|) :
    FDR H₀ (knockoffRejects W α) μ ≤ α
formalizationNotes: The Lean statement adds two regularity hypotheses beyond the bare book statement, both holding automatically for continuous knock-off statistics: null statistics are a.s. nonzero (so the sign is well defined) and magnitudes are a.s. distinct (so the threshold ordering is unambiguous). The 1 + V_- denominator is the +1 of the knock-off+ procedure that yields exact FDR ≤ α control.

hypotheses.label: knock-off score
hypotheses.note: W satisfies the sign-symmetry / knock-off-score assumption (null statistics have symmetric signs).

hypotheses.label: no null ties
hypotheses.note: Each null statistic W_j is almost surely nonzero, so its sign is well defined.

hypotheses.label: distinct magnitudes
hypotheses.note: The magnitudes |W_i| are almost surely pairwise distinct (no ties to break).

reference.formal: Junwei Lu, *Big Data Analysis*, Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025.
reference.biblio: The knock-off filter originates with R. F. Barber and E. J. Candès, "Controlling the false discovery rate via knockoffs", *Annals of Statistics* **43**(5):2055–2085, 2015 (arXiv:1404.5609). That paper's Theorem 1 controls a *modified* FDR for the plain knock-off procedure, while its Theorem 2 establishes exact $\mathrm{FDR} \le q$ control for the knock-off$^+$ procedure — the variant with the "$+1$" offset in the FDP estimate that is formalized here.

title: Kolmogorov–Smirnov Test Level
informal:
The one-sided Kolmogorov–Smirnov test of the global null rejects when the one-sided KS statistic $\mathrm{KS}^{+} = \sup_{t} (F_n(t) - t)$ exceeds the threshold $u_\alpha = \sqrt{\log(n/\alpha)/(2n)}$, where $F_n$ is the empirical CDF of $n$ p-values.

Under the global null — the $n$ p-values are jointly independent and each is super-uniform, its CDF lying below the uniform CDF — the test has level $\alpha$:

$$ \mu\bigl\{\, \mathrm{KS}^{+} \ge u_\alpha \,\bigr\} \;\le\; \alpha . $$
summary: The one-sided Kolmogorov-Smirnov test that rejects when KS+ exceeds the union-bound threshold has type-I error at most alpha under the global null.
leanSignature:
theorem ks_test_level {n : ℕ} (hn : 0 < n) (μ : Measure Ω) [IsProbabilityMeasure μ]
    (p : Fin n → Ω → ℝ)
    (hmeas : ∀ j, Measurable (p j))
    (hindep : iIndepFun p μ)
    (hnull : ∀ j, SuperUniform (p j) μ)
    {α : ℝ} (hα0 : 0 < α) (hα1 : α < 1) :
    μ {ω | Real.sqrt (Real.log ((n : ℝ) / α) / (2 * n)) ≤ ksPlus p ω} ≤ ENNReal.ofReal α
formalizationNotes: The sharp Dvoretzky–Kiefer–Wolfowitz–Massart constant would let the threshold improve to √(log(2/α)/(2n)); the version proved here uses the (weaker) union-bound tail, which is the inequality actually available in the library, giving threshold √(log(n/α)/(2n)).

hypotheses.label: independence
hypotheses.note: The n p-values are jointly independent under μ.

hypotheses.label: super-uniform nulls
hypotheses.note: Each p-value is super-uniform: its CDF lies below the uniform CDF, P(p_j ≤ t) ≤ t.

reference.formal: E. J. Candès, *STAT 300C: Theory of Statistics*, Lecture Notes, Stanford University.
reference.biblio: The two-sided KS statistic and its limiting distribution originate with A. N. Kolmogorov, "Sulla determinazione empirica di una legge di distribuzione," *Giornale dell'Istituto Italiano degli Attuari* **4** (1933), 83–91. N. V. Smirnov, "Table for estimating the goodness of fit of empirical distributions," *Annals of Mathematical Statistics* **19** (1948), 279–281, tabulated the limiting distribution and studied the two-sample form. The non-asymptotic exponential tail bound used here is the Dvoretzky–Kiefer–Wolfowitz inequality — A. Dvoretzky, J. Kiefer, and J. Wolfowitz, "Asymptotic minimax character of the sample distribution function and of the classical multinomial estimator," *Annals of Mathematical Statistics* **27** (1956), 642–669 — with the sharp leading constant established by P. Massart, "The tight constant in the Dvoretzky–Kiefer–Wolfowitz inequality," *Annals of Probability* **18** (1990), 1269–1283.

title: Chi-Squared Statistic Mean under H₀
informal:
In the Gaussian sequence model the chi-squared statistic under the null $H_0$ is $T_n = \sum_{i=1}^n z_i^2$.

If each $z_i \sim N(0,1)$, then $$\mathbb{E}[T_n] = n.$$
summary: Under the null, the chi-squared statistic sum of z_i squared has expectation n for standard Gaussian z_i.

theorem chiSq_H0_mean (P : Measure Ω) [IsProbabilityMeasure P] (z : Fin n → Ω → ℝ)
    (hmeas : ∀ i, Measurable (z i))
    (hlaw : ∀ i, Measure.map (z i) P = gaussianReal 0 1) :
    ∫ ω, ∑ i, (z i ω) ^ 2 ∂P = (n : ℝ)

hypotheses.label: standard Gaussian
hypotheses.note: Each coordinate z_i has law N(0,1) under P.

reference.formal: E. J. Candès, *STAT 300C: Theory of Statistics*, Lecture Notes, Stanford University.
reference.biblio: The chi-squared goodness-of-fit statistic originates with K. Pearson, "On the criterion that a given system of deviations from the probable in the case of a correlated system of variables is such that it can be reasonably supposed to have arisen from random sampling," *Philosophical Magazine*, Series 5, **50** (1900), 157–175. The mean and variance of $\chi^2_n$ ($n$ and $2n$) are standard moment computations; the Candès lecture notes apply them to the Gaussian-sequence power analysis.

if each $z_i \sim N(0,1)$ and the $z_i$ are jointly independent, then $$\operatorname{Var}[T_n] = 2n.$$
